mnemonics.title: Mnemonics & Memory Hacks
mnemonics.description: Retain key features and article scopes of Part III using simple memory tricks.

items.title: Mnemonic 1
items.decryption: Categories of rights: Freedom (Articles 19-22), Religion (Articles 25-28), Equality (Articles 14-18), Saving of certain laws (Articles 31A-31C), Culture/Education (Articles 29-30), Opposing Exploitation (Articles 23-24).

items.title: Mnemonic 2
items.decryption: Remember that Article 12 defines the State (the entity against which rights are enforced), and Article 13 declares laws inconsistent with FRs as Void.

items.title: Mnemonic 3
items.decryption: During a National Emergency, all Fundamental Rights can be suspended except Articles 20 and 21 (added by the 44th Amendment Act, 1978).

items.question: Which part of the Indian Constitution is described as the 'Magna Carta of India'?
items.answer: Part III of the Constitution, which contains the Fundamental Rights (Articles 12 to 35).

items.question: Are Fundamental Rights absolute in nature?
items.answer: No. They are not absolute but qualified. The State can impose reasonable restrictions on them, subject to judicial review.

items.question: Which Fundamental Right was deleted by the 44th Amendment Act, 1978?
items.answer: The Right to Property (Article 31). It was made a legal/constitutional right under Article 300A in Part XII.

items.question: Against whom are Fundamental Rights primarily available?
items.answer: They are primarily available against the arbitrary action of the State (as defined under Article 12). However, some rights are also available against private individuals (e.g., Articles 17, 23, and 24).

items.question: Can judicial review under Article 13 declare a constitutional amendment act void?
items.answer: In the Kesavananda Bharati case (1973), the Supreme Court held that a constitutional amendment can be challenged on the ground that it violates the 'Basic Structure' of the Constitution.

traps.title: UPSC Civil Services Exam Traps to Avoid
items: Trap 1: Believing all Fundamental Rights are available to foreigners. Note that Articles 15, 16, 19, 29, and 30 are available exclusively to citizens of India, while the rest are available to all persons (citizens or foreigners).

Trap 2: Assuming 'State' under Article 12 only includes government departments. It also includes local authorities (Panchayats, Municipalities) and statutory/non-statutory authorities performing public duties (e.g., LIC, ONGC, SAIL).

Trap 3: Confusing the effect of Article 13. Remember that pre-constitutional laws inconsistent with FRs are not void ab initio (void from the beginning), but only become inoperative to the extent of inconsistency under the Doctrine of Eclipse.

sections.title: 1. Meaning, Classifications & Core Characteristics of Part III
sections.content:
Introduction to Part III

Part III is called the 'Magna Carta of India'. The rights are called 'Fundamental' because they are guaranteed and protected by the Constitution, which is the fundamental law of the land. They are essential for the overall development (material, intellectual, moral, and spiritual) of individuals.

Core Characteristics of Fundamental Rights:

  • Justiciability: Enforceable directly in courts. Persons can directly approach the Supreme Court (under Article 32) or High Courts (under Article 226) if their rights are violated.
  • State vs Private Action: Most are available against the state, but some (like prohibition of untouchability and forced labor) bind private individuals as well.
  • Not Sacrosanct or Permanent: Parliament can curtail or repeal them by a constitutional amendment act under Article 368, without altering the 'Basic Structure'.
  • Suspension: Can be suspended during a National Emergency (except Articles 20 and 21). Article 19 can only be suspended during emergency declared on grounds of war or external aggression.

sections.title: 2. Foundation Articles - Article 12 (State) & Article 13 (Judicial Review)
sections.content:
Article 12: Definition of 'State'

To avoid ambiguity regarding against whom these rights are enforceable, Article 12 defines 'State' broadly to include: (a) Government and Parliament of India, (b) Government and Legislature of states, (c) All local authorities (municipalities, panchayats), and (d) Other authorities (statutory like LIC, ONGC, non-statutory performing public roles).

Article 13: Laws Inconsistent with Fundamental Rights

Article 13 provides the constitutional base for Judicial Review. It declares that all laws that are inconsistent with or in derogation of any of the fundamental rights shall be void. This covers permanent laws, temporary laws (ordinances), and non-legislative sources (customs or usage).

Doctrine (Derived from Art 13)Definition / MeaningApplication
Doctrine of SeverabilityOnly the offending part of a law is declared void, not the entire law, if they can be separated.Saves valid parts of laws from being struck down.
Doctrine of EclipsePre-constitutional laws inconsistent with FRs remain dormant (eclipsed) but not dead. If FR is amended, eclipse is removed.Applies to pre-constitutional laws; later extended in some cases.
Doctrine of WaiverCitizens cannot waive off (give up) their Fundamental Rights as they are matters of public policy.Ensures protection of rights regardless of personal choice.

sections.title: 3. Evolution, Importance & Constitutional Safeguards of Part III
sections.content:
Significance and Importance

Fundamental Rights prevent the establishment of authoritarian rule and protect individual liberties against State encroachment. They establish "a government of laws and not of men". They are crucial for preserving human dignity, individual freedom, and maintaining minority interests within the democracy.

Exceptions and Limitations

  • Article 31A: Saves laws providing for acquisition of estates from being challenged under Articles 14 and 19.
  • Article 31B: Saves acts in the Ninth Schedule from judicial review (though the SC in I.R. Coelho Case, 2007 ruled that acts added after April 24, 1973, are open to challenge if they violate the basic structure).
  • Article 31C: Saves laws giving effect to Directive Principles under Article 39(b) and 39(c).
  • Military Limitations (Article 33 & 34): Parliament can restrict or abrogate the FRs of members of the armed forces, police forces, and intelligence agencies to ensure discipline. Martial law (Rule of military) allows abrogation of rights in specified areas.
